scenarios.title: Tanker leak at I-95 mile 22
scenarios.outcomeType: Decision sequence — isolate, communicate, request resources

welcome.title: Scenario overview
welcome.body: You are an Engine 4 firefighter responding to a single-vehicle incident on I-95. Today we focus on isolation discipline.
welcome.reassurance: We aren't testing you; we're rehearsing the muscle memory you need when minutes matter.
welcome.expectedOutcome: Demonstrate isolation, communication, and clean handoff under pressure.

scenarios.context: Light mist drifting across the southbound lanes. UN 1203 placards visible. Wind SW ~10 mph. Two vehicles stopped within 30m.

steps.title: First 60 seconds
steps.prompt: What do you do?
steps.coachHint: Start with what protects everyone — including you.

options.label: Approach the tanker to read the BOL
options.feedback: You closed the gap before establishing isolation — this is how responders become patients.
options.insight: You closed the gap to gather information before establishing safety.

options.label: Establish 50m isolation upwind, hold position
options.feedback: Good. You bought yourself a thinking margin and protected the bystanders downwind.
options.insight: You prioritized spatial safety immediately.

options.label: Begin moving stopped vehicles
options.feedback: Reasonable instinct, but isolation comes first.
options.insight: You moved to protect bystanders, but exposed yourself before setting the perimeter.

steps.title: Sitrep to dispatch
steps.prompt: Compose the sitrep. Lead with the picture, not the timeline.
steps.voicePrompt: Engine 4 on scene I-95 southbound mile 22, single tanker UN 1203, active leak with vapor, wind south-west ten, fifty meter isolation set, requesting hazmat one and PD for traffic.
steps.coachHint: Be specific. Location, product, hazard, wind, isolation, resources.
steps.modelAnswer: Engine 4 on scene I-95 SB mile 22, single tanker UN 1203, active leak with vapor, wind SW 10, 50m isolation set, requesting hazmat 1 and PD for traffic.

scenarios.title: Class debate · structuring a counter-argument
scenarios.outcomeType: Build a claim → evidence → warrant chain under time pressure.

welcome.title: Scenario overview
welcome.body: You're prepping for a class debate. Your opponent just posted their opening: "Remote learning hurts students — the latest test scores are down 12% nationally." You have five minutes to draft a counter.
welcome.highlight: Most weak counters attack the conclusion before testing the warrant.
welcome.reassurance: We aren't grading the rhetoric — we're rehearsing how you separate claim, evidence, and warrant.
welcome.expectedOutcome: Identify the weak link in the argument, then frame a counter that holds up.

scenarios.context: Five minutes on the clock. The opening claim cites one national figure and treats it as proof. Your counter needs to land in two paragraphs.

steps.title: Where is the argument weakest?
steps.prompt: Pick the gap your counter should attack first.
steps.coachHint: Claim, evidence, warrant — which one isn't holding up the weight?

options.label: The claim itself — remote learning isn't actually harmful
options.feedback: You're swinging at the conclusion without first checking whether the evidence even supports it. That's the trap.
options.insight: You attacked the claim before testing the chain that holds it up.

options.label: The warrant — one test-score number doesn't prove the cause is remote learning
options.feedback: Right. The evidence may be real, but the leap from "scores dropped" to "remote learning caused it" is the unspoken warrant — and it doesn't hold without controls.
options.insight: You named the missing warrant — the assumption doing the work in silence.

options.label: The evidence — the 12% figure is probably wrong
options.feedback: Possible, but you'd need a counter-source. Attacking the warrant is faster and stronger when the data is hard to dispute.
options.insight: You went after the data, which is defensible but slower than attacking the logic.

steps.title: Frame your counter
steps.prompt: Pick the strongest opening move for your counter-argument.
steps.coachHint: A good counter concedes what's true, then narrows the disagreement.

options.label: "Scores did drop, but the cause isn't remote learning — it's the disruption itself. Here's evidence that scores also dropped in districts that stayed in-person."
options.feedback: Strong. You conceded the evidence, isolated the warrant, and offered a competing explanation with its own support.
options.insight: You used a concede-then-narrow move — the structure judges look for.

options.label: "That 12% figure is from a single source and shouldn't be trusted."
options.feedback: Source critique is fair, but without a stronger source of your own you've only created doubt, not a counter.
options.insight: You raised credibility doubt without offering a competing position.

options.label: "Remote learning has real benefits, like flexibility and accessibility."
options.feedback: You changed the subject. The opening was about a causal claim — pivoting to benefits doesn't refute it, it talks past it.
options.insight: You pivoted to a different argument instead of engaging the one on the table.

scenarios.title: Conveyor LOTO · pre-maintenance lockout
scenarios.outcomeType: Sequence the six-step LOTO before service work begins.

welcome.title: Scenario overview
welcome.body: Line 3 conveyor needs a bearing replaced. The shift lead has cleared the line and handed it off to you for lockout before maintenance can begin.
welcome.highlight: Skipping verify is behind most stored-energy injuries.
welcome.reassurance: We aren't testing speed — we're rehearsing the sequence so it's automatic when the line is loud.
welcome.expectedOutcome: Run the six steps in order — and verify before anyone touches the equipment.

scenarios.context: Line 3 is powered down at the local control panel. The maintenance tech is gloved up, waiting on you. Two other shifts share this line.

steps.title: The line is stopped. What's next?
steps.prompt: What's your next action before maintenance can start?
steps.coachHint: Stopping the line is not the same as isolating it.

options.label: Hand the line over — it's already stopped at the local control
options.feedback: Local control is not isolation. The conveyor can be restarted from another panel — or backfed if someone resets the breaker.
options.insight: You treated a stopped line as a safe line. Stopped is not isolated.

options.label: Isolate at the disconnect, apply your personal lock, then dissipate stored energy
options.feedback: Correct. Isolate → lock → dissipate is the heart of the sequence. Your lock — not the lead's, not the tech's — owns this isolation.
options.insight: You ran the sequence correctly and kept ownership of the lock on your name.

options.label: Lock the local control panel and have the tech start work
options.feedback: Locking the control isn't isolating the energy source. The motor still has a feed; the system still has stored energy.
options.insight: You locked the wrong device — controls are not isolation points.

steps.title: Lock is on. Tech is ready.
steps.prompt: The tech reaches for the bearing. What do you do first?
steps.coachHint: The last step is the one most often skipped.

options.label: Attempt to start the conveyor at the local panel — confirm it's dead
options.feedback: That's verification. You proved zero energy by attempting normal operation. Now work can start.
options.insight: You verified by test — the only step that actually proves the lock did its job.

options.label: Wave the tech in — the lock is on, that's the verification
options.feedback: A lock proves intent, not state. Verify the equipment is actually de-energized before anyone reaches in.
options.insight: You skipped verify. Locks fail; stored energy hides.

options.label: Check the disconnect is in the off position one more time
options.feedback: Better than nothing, but visual confirmation isn't the same as a function test. Attempt a start to truly verify.
options.insight: You re-checked visually but didn't prove zero energy by test.

scenarios.title: 78F, altered, fever — triage decision
scenarios.outcomeType: Recognition + bundle initiation timeline

welcome.title: Scenario overview
welcome.body: 78F arrives in triage from a SNF. Family reports a day of confusion and "just not herself." Vitals: T 38.6, HR 112, RR 24, BP 96/58, SpO2 94%.
welcome.highlight: qSOFA is a flag, not a diagnosis.
welcome.reassurance: We aren't grading speed — we're rehearsing the recognition pattern so the hour-1 clock starts on time.
welcome.expectedOutcome: Recognize early sepsis, start the bundle in the right order, and escalate when the response is inadequate.

scenarios.context: Lobby's full. The patient is awake but slow to answer. No known infection source yet. Provider available bedside.

steps.title: Is this sepsis?
steps.prompt: How do you flag this patient?
steps.coachHint: Two of three on qSOFA — RR ≥22, altered mentation, SBP ≤100.

options.label: Routine ESI 3 — fever, get a workup going
options.feedback: She meets three qSOFA criteria with hypotension. Routine triage delays the hour-1 clock; this needs the sepsis pathway now.
options.insight: You missed the qSOFA pattern and routed her into a slower lane.

options.label: Flag for sepsis pathway — qSOFA positive, start the hour-1 clock
options.feedback: Right. Three of three qSOFA with hypotension is a clear flag. The clock starts now, not when culture results come back.
options.insight: You recognized the pattern early and protected the bundle timeline.

options.label: Hold for provider eval before deciding pathway
options.feedback: The provider is available bedside — loop them in, but don't wait to flag. The pathway is yours to initiate at the bedside.
options.insight: You deferred a recognition you were qualified to make, costing minutes on the bundle.

steps.title: Bundle is open. What goes first?
steps.prompt: Pick the next action that actually moves the hour-1 bundle forward.
steps.coachHint: Cultures before antibiotics, fluids early, lactate to anchor the response.

options.label: Draw lactate and blood cultures, then start broad-spectrum antibiotics; begin 30 mL/kg crystalloid
options.feedback: Textbook hour-1 order. Cultures protect future ID work, antibiotics don't wait on culture results, and the fluid bolus starts addressing perfusion.
options.insight: You sequenced the bundle correctly — cultures before antibiotics, fluids in parallel.

options.label: Start antibiotics immediately, draw cultures after they're hung
options.feedback: Antibiotics first protects the patient but compromises culture yield — and the order matters for downstream ID. Draw first when you can.
options.insight: You prioritized the patient over the workup. Defensible, but the bundle expects cultures first.

options.label: Hold antibiotics until cultures result so coverage is targeted
options.feedback: Hour-1 doesn't wait for culture results — every hour of delayed antibiotics in septic shock raises mortality measurably.
options.insight: You waited for certainty in a clock that doesn't allow it.

scenarios.title: Routine medical call · single patient
scenarios.outcomeType: Scene safety, vitals, communication

welcome.title: Scenario overview
welcome.body: Dispatched for a 58-year-old with chest discomfort. Front porch. Spouse on scene. Patient is conscious and talking.
welcome.highlight: Read the scene before you touch the patient.
welcome.reassurance: This is a rehearsal, not a test. There's no penalty for taking your time.
welcome.expectedOutcome: Run a clean primary assessment and communicate clearly with the patient.

scenarios.context: Quiet residential street, daylight. No hazards visible. Spouse is anxious but coherent. Patient is seated, pale, diaphoretic, breathing about 22.

dispatch.text: Medic 7, respond priority one to 412 Linden Court for a fifty-eight-year-old male, chest pain and shortness of breath, conscious and breathing. Spouse on scene. No known cardiac history. Cross street Maple. Time out, fourteen twenty-two.

steps.title: First contact
steps.prompt: How do you approach the patient?
steps.coachHint: Your opening shapes the next ten minutes.

options.label: Squat to eye level, introduce yourself, ask what's going on
options.feedback: Right tone — you lowered the stress level before asking for information.
options.insight: You set a calm tone before assessment, which makes the history more reliable.

options.label: Open with vitals immediately — slap on the BP cuff
options.feedback: Workable, but you skipped the trust step. History gets thinner when patients feel processed.
options.insight: You moved to data before rapport.

options.label: Talk to the spouse first, the patient is breathing fine
options.feedback: The patient is conscious — they're your source of truth.
options.insight: You bypassed the patient as the primary witness.

steps.title: What do you check first?
steps.prompt: Which assessment do you run first?
steps.coachHint: ABCs before anything diagnostic.

options.label: Airway, breathing, circulation, then focused history
options.feedback: Textbook — and the right call. You catch surprises before they catch you.
options.insight: You ran the primary in order, which is what stays reliable under stress.

options.label: Jump straight to 12-lead ECG
options.feedback: Useful diagnostic, but you skipped the primary. A patient with an unstable airway doesn't care about ST elevation.
options.insight: You went diagnostic before stabilization.

options.label: Take a detailed history, vitals can wait
options.feedback: History is valuable, but vitals are your trend line. You'll miss the deterioration.
options.insight: You delayed the data that catches decline.

steps.title: Update the patient
steps.prompt: The patient asks if it's a heart attack. What do you say?
steps.coachHint: Honest, not alarming.

options.label: "I can't say for sure — but your symptoms match a few things we treat early, so we're going to move quickly."
options.feedback: Honest, calm, and gives them a frame. That's what they'll remember.
options.insight: You held the uncertainty without amplifying fear.

options.label: "No, you're fine."
options.feedback: You can't say that — and if you're wrong, you'll lose the trust you need.
options.insight: You over-reassured beyond what you can know.

options.label: "Yes, this looks like a heart attack."
options.feedback: You're not the one diagnosing in this moment. Naming it without proof can do harm.
options.insight: You overcommitted to a diagnosis you don't yet have.

scenarios.title: Multi-unit response · evolving condition
scenarios.outcomeType: Handoff, radio discipline, and reprioritization

welcome.title: Scenario overview
welcome.body: You're on a multi-unit MVC. Two patients, one critical. Engine 7 is en route, you're holding the radio.
welcome.reassurance: Different setup than your last run — same skills, more moving parts.
welcome.expectedOutcome: Reprioritize cleanly, hand off without losing the picture.

scenarios.context: Two-car crash, intersection. Patient A: head impact, GCS 13, neck pain. Patient B: ambulatory, anxious, complaining of arm pain. PD on scene, traffic blocked.

steps.title: Who gets your attention first?
steps.prompt: How do you prioritize?
steps.coachHint: Worst first, by physiology — not by who's loudest.

options.label: Patient A — head impact, altered GCS
options.feedback: Right call. The quiet patient is usually the sicker one.
options.insight: You weighted physiology over volume.

options.label: Patient B — they're more vocal, easier to assess
options.feedback: You anchored on accessibility. The head-impact patient is your priority.
options.insight: You anchored on the easier patient, not the sicker one.

options.label: Split — partner takes A, you take B
options.feedback: Defensible if your partner is independent, but you lose the unified picture.
options.insight: You distributed attention rather than concentrating it on the worst patient.

steps.title: Update to Engine 7 inbound
steps.prompt: Compose the inbound update. Lead with the picture.
steps.voicePrompt: Medic four at fifth and main, two patients from MVC, patient A altered GCS thirteen with head impact priority one, patient B ambulatory arm pain priority two, requesting one additional ALS unit for transport.
steps.coachHint: Location, patients, priority, ask.
steps.modelAnswer: Medic 4 at 5th & Main, 2 pts MVC. Pt A: GCS 13, head impact, P1. Pt B: ambulatory, arm pain, P2. Requesting one additional ALS unit for transport.

steps.title: Condition change
steps.prompt: Patient A's GCS just dropped to 10. What now?
steps.coachHint: Stay calm, narrow the field.

options.label: Update radio, expedite transport, prep for airway management
options.feedback: Clean. You reacted to the trend, not the number.
options.insight: You moved on a trend, which is what catches deterioration in time.

options.label: Hold position, recheck in 5 minutes
options.feedback: A dropping GCS doesn't wait.
options.insight: You held in a window that required forward motion.

options.label: Transfer A to Engine 7's care, focus on B
options.feedback: You'd hand off your critical patient mid-deterioration — that's where errors live.
options.insight: You handed off your hardest patient at the worst moment.

scenarios.title: Compounding scene · stress decision drill
scenarios.outcomeType: Decide under stress when the scene is changing

welcome.title: Scenario overview
welcome.body: Single patient turns into three. PD is asking for direction. You have one partner. Decide.
welcome.reassurance: Adapted from your prior practice — you've already shown the foundation here.
welcome.expectedOutcome: Narrow the field and commit, even when the picture is incomplete.

scenarios.context: Single-patient call became a brawl on arrival. Three potential patients, PD requesting EMS direction, your partner is occupied.

steps.title: First move
steps.prompt: What do you do?
steps.coachHint: Pick the next-best action you can defend in 10 seconds.

options.label: Call for a second unit, START-triage the three patients
options.feedback: Right call — you built the structure that scales.
options.insight: You bought structure under load.

options.label: Take the loudest patient first, send partner to a quieter one
options.feedback: Volume isn't a triage variable.
options.insight: You weighted attention by volume.

options.label: Wait for PD to clear the scene before assessing
options.feedback: Defensible if there's an active threat — but you've lost time and the picture.
options.insight: You traded data for safety, which is sometimes right and sometimes a miss.

steps.title: PD asks what they need
steps.prompt: PD is asking what to do. Your answer?
steps.coachHint: Short, clear, actionable.

options.label: "Hold the perimeter. I'll triage; you keep bystanders at 30 feet."
options.feedback: Direct, scoped, executable. Exactly what they need.
options.insight: You gave a single executable instruction.

options.label: "Whatever you think."
options.feedback: You're the EMS lead — they're asking you because the call is yours.
options.insight: You deferred when leadership was needed.

options.label: Long explanation of triage methodology
options.feedback: Right content, wrong moment. Compress it to one instruction.
options.insight: You explained when you should have directed.

scenarios.title: New airway & cardiac protocol drill
scenarios.outcomeType: Apply the updated airway/cardiac sequence

welcome.title: Scenario overview
welcome.body: Run the new airway and cardiac arrest sequence. Same patient your service has run a hundred times — different protocol.
welcome.reassurance: The new protocol changes timing, not principles. We'll walk it.
welcome.expectedOutcome: Apply the updated sequence cleanly and explain the change.

scenarios.context: Adult cardiac arrest, witnessed. Bystander CPR in progress. AED applied, no shock advised on first analysis.

steps.title: What's the first protocol change?
steps.prompt: Under the new sequence, what do you do first after taking over CPR?
steps.coachHint: The new protocol delays a step you used to do early.

options.label: Continue compressions, delay advanced airway until first rhythm check
options.feedback: Right — early advanced airway moved later in the new sequence.
options.insight: You applied the new timing correctly.

options.label: Place advanced airway immediately
options.feedback: Old protocol. The new sequence delays this to preserve compression continuity.
options.insight: You ran the old sequence.

options.label: Skip compressions, prep for transport
options.feedback: Compressions are the work — never skip them.
options.insight: You bypassed the core intervention.

steps.title: Rhythm check
steps.prompt: First analysis: organized rhythm, no pulse. Next action?
steps.coachHint: Stick to the new algorithm.

options.label: Resume CPR, push epi per new interval
options.feedback: Correct — PEA pathway, with the new epi timing.
options.insight: You stayed on the new pathway.

options.label: Shock now
options.feedback: PEA isn't shockable.
options.insight: You moved off the algorithm.

options.label: Pause everything, call medical control
options.feedback: Medical control is a resource, not a substitute for the algorithm.
options.insight: You substituted consultation for execution.

scenarios.title: A party, a friend, a moment to act
scenarios.outcomeType: Step in as a bystander before the situation escalates

welcome.title: Scenario overview
welcome.body: You're at an off-campus party. Sam — someone from your stats class, but not really a friend — is several drinks in and the night is heading toward a decision point. You'll talk it through with Coach Vic in your own words, by text or voice.
welcome.reassurance: This is rehearsal, not assessment — there's no single right path. You can take your time.
welcome.expectedOutcome: Read the room, use your judgment, and decide what (if anything) you'll do.

scenarios.context: House party, around midnight. Sam — a classmate you know from your stats class, but not really a friend — has been drinking heavily for a couple of hours. They're getting louder, less steady, and starting to argue with someone they barely know.

keyframe.caption: Midnight. Sam's loud, unsteady, and arguing with a stranger.

beats.prompt: You're at the party and you spot Sam — that classmate from stats, not really a friend — pretty drunk and getting into it with someone they barely know. What's your read on what's happening here, and is this yours to do anything about?

consider.t: You're barely friends — someone closer to Sam should handle it
It's just drunk-and-loud, not actually dangerous
That argument could turn into something — that's the real risk

reply.act: Fair — 'I barely know them' and 'this could go bad' can both be true at once. Not knowing Sam well doesn't make you the wrong person; it makes you the person who's actually here. Let's see what you do with that.
reply.defer: That's the honest first reaction — they're not your friend, so why you? Hold that thought, because the night isn't going to wait for the 'right' person to show up.

keyframe.caption: It tips over — a shove, raised voices, people backing away.

beats.prompt: You hang back. A minute later it tips over — Sam shoves the guy, voices spike, people start backing off. Still not yours? What do you do now?

consider.t: Now it's a fight, not my mess — let it play out
Step in and try to defuse it
Find someone who actually knows Sam

reply.act: Right — waiting made it harder, not easier. Let's get you in there.
reply.find: Smart instinct — someone Sam trusts would land better than a stranger. Let's see if you can find them.
reply.defer: It's escalating and still nobody's moved. This is the part where 'someone else' quietly turns out to be you.

keyframe.caption: Sam grabs their keys and heads for the lot — alone, wrecked.

beats.prompt: Nobody stepped in. Now Sam's done with the party — keys out, heading for the parking lot to drive home, barely walking straight. This is the last clean chance. What do you do?

consider.t: Go after Sam and stop them driving
Tell someone at the party that Sam's leaving
It's their call — they're an adult

reply.act: Good — this is the one that actually matters. A drunk drive is the outcome this whole night was sliding toward, and you just cut it off.
reply.defer: And that's where it ends — you let it ride all the way to someone drunk behind a wheel.

keyframe.caption: You've decided to step in. How you do it matters.

beats.prompt: You've decided to do something. Sam's drunk, a little wound up, and barely knows you. How do you actually approach this without it blowing up?

consider.t: Pull Sam aside quietly and check in
Find one of Sam's actual friends to take the lead
Say it loud so everyone helps shut it down

reply.direct: Good call — low-key and private keeps Sam's back from going up. Dignity intact, defenses down.
reply.find: Reasonable — someone Sam trusts can land this better than you can. Let's see if you can actually find them.
reply.confront: Careful — calling it out in front of everyone usually backfires. A drunk person who feels cornered digs in. Watch what happens.

keyframe.caption: You scan the party for someone who actually knows Sam.

beats.prompt: You go looking for someone closer to Sam — honestly, the right move. But you push through the crowd and… you don't really know Sam's friends, and the two people you ask just shrug and turn back to their drinks. There's no one. It's on you. What now?

consider.t: Go back and talk to Sam yourself
Ask the host to help you get Sam home
You tried — leave it to the room

reply.direct: That's the whole point of this moment: looking for the right person was smart — but when there isn't one, 'I tried' doesn't get Sam home. You're up.
reply.defer: Trying counts for something — but Sam's still here and still in trouble. 'I looked for someone' isn't the same as 'I helped.'

keyframe.caption: You called it out. Sam's humiliated — and digging in.

beats.prompt: You said it loud. Now Sam's embarrassed in front of everyone and getting defensive — 'I'm FINE, back off.' It got worse. How do you bring it back down?

consider.t: Drop the volume and pull Sam aside now
Double down — they need to hear it
Find someone Sam trusts to smooth it over

reply.direct: Better. You can't un-embarrass them, but dropping the volume and going private gives Sam a way to climb down.
reply.find: Worth a shot — a familiar face can de-escalate what you stirred up.
reply.confront: Doubling down on a humiliated, drunk person is how this turns into a real fight.

keyframe.caption: Sam's with you now — guard half up. The next words matter.

beats.prompt: Sam's actually listening now, a little defensive. In your own words: what do you say to get them out of here safely — without making them feel judged?

reply.good: That lands — warm, specific, and it gives Sam an exit that doesn't feel like a verdict. That's the whole skill.

keyframe.caption: Sam's in a ride home. Handled.

beats.prompt: Sam got home safe — because you treated 'not my close friend' as 'still worth doing something about.' Here's how your read held up.

keyframe.caption: The party winds down. You'll never know how Sam's night ended.

beats.prompt: You stayed out of it the whole way. Maybe Sam was fine. Maybe not — and that not-knowing is the cost of waiting for someone else to act. Let's look at where you could've stepped in.

steps.title: What are you actually seeing?
steps.prompt: Which read of the situation matches what you're seeing?
steps.coachHint: Look for cues you'd describe out loud — slurred speech, balance, escalation.

options.label: High-risk impairment — Sam's judgment is gone, and the argument could escalate
options.feedback: You're naming the cues correctly. That's the read that justifies stepping in.
options.insight: You used the impairment cues to size up the risk.

options.label: Normal party energy — they'll sleep it off
options.feedback: The cues add up to more than "normal party energy." Naming that out loud is what unlocks action.
options.insight: You under-read the cues.

options.label: Not your business — Sam's an adult
options.feedback: "Adult" isn't the question. The question is whether the next 10 minutes could go badly without a friend in the room.
options.insight: You opted out of responsibility too early.

steps.title: How do you step in?
steps.prompt: What's your move?
steps.coachHint: Low-friction first — direct, distract, or delegate. Keep Sam's dignity intact.

options.label: Pull Sam aside with a low-key excuse and check in
options.feedback: The "distract" move keeps Sam's dignity intact and buys you a chance to actually talk.
options.insight: You picked the lowest-friction intervention.

options.label: Call them out in front of the group
options.feedback: Public callouts usually escalate, not de-escalate. Save it for when nothing else works.
options.insight: You escalated when de-escalation was available.

options.label: Do nothing — someone else will handle it
options.feedback: The bystander effect runs the rest of the night when no one takes the first step.
options.insight: You diffused responsibility.

steps.title: What do you actually say?
steps.prompt: Write the line you'd say to Sam to get them out of the argument and somewhere safer.
steps.coachHint: Short, warm, no judgment. Give Sam a graceful exit.
steps.voicePrompt: Hey Sam — Maya was looking for you in the kitchen. Walk with me for a sec?
steps.modelAnswer: Hey Sam — Maya was looking for you in the kitchen. Walk with me for a sec? I'm grabbing water anyway.
rubric: Moves them physically away from the flashpoint

scenarios.title: Keys in the parking lot
scenarios.outcomeType: Stop a friend from getting in a car with an impaired driver

welcome.title: Scenario overview
welcome.body: You're outside the party. A classmate is about to get in the passenger seat of a car driven by someone who's clearly been drinking. You have about thirty seconds.
welcome.reassurance: This is rehearsal. The cost of trying the wrong line here is nothing.
welcome.expectedOutcome: Interrupt the handoff and offer a real alternative.

scenarios.context: 1:15 a.m. Cold parking lot. Your classmate Alex is reaching for the passenger door. The driver, someone Alex met an hour ago, is fumbling with their keys.

steps.title: What do you do first?
steps.prompt: You have one move before that door closes. What is it?
steps.coachHint: Direct beats clever here. Use Alex's name.

options.label: Step in, use Alex's name, and offer to walk them to a rideshare
options.feedback: Direct + specific alternative. That's the move when time is short.
options.insight: You combined interruption with a real alternative.

options.label: Argue with the driver about whether they're safe to drive
options.feedback: You're trying — but arguing with the driver leaves Alex still standing at the door. Talk to Alex.
options.insight: You aimed at the wrong person.

options.label: Yell at them both to stop
options.feedback: Yelling makes Alex defensive and locks the decision in.
options.insight: You escalated tone instead of changing the choice.

steps.title: What's the alternative?
steps.prompt: Alex hesitates. What do you offer?
steps.coachHint: Make the alternative as easy as the bad option.

options.label: "I'm calling a rideshare right now — we'll split it, two minutes."
options.feedback: Concrete, immediate, low-friction. That's the offer that wins.
options.insight: You made the safe option the easy option.

options.label: "You shouldn't get in that car."
options.feedback: True but not enough — they need a path, not just a warning.
options.insight: You named the risk without offering a path.

options.label: "Fine — text me when you're home."
options.feedback: That's not a handoff, it's a hope.
options.insight: You handed responsibility back to chance.

steps.title: What would you say afterward?
steps.prompt: Write the short follow-up you'd send Alex the next day.
steps.coachHint: Warm, no lecture. Make it easy for Alex to talk to you again.
steps.voicePrompt: Hey — glad we grabbed that ride last night. No big deal, just wanted to check you got some sleep.
steps.modelAnswer: Hey — glad we grabbed that ride last night. No big deal, just wanted to check you got some sleep.

scenarios.title: Picking sources for a 5-page paper
scenarios.outcomeType: Evaluate three sources fast

welcome.title: Scenario overview
welcome.body: You have an assignment due in 36 hours. You have three potential sources open in tabs. Pick the ones you can defend in your works-cited.
welcome.reassurance: This is rehearsal, not assessment. You can take the time to read each source.
welcome.expectedOutcome: Sort credible from questionable using the 30-second check.

scenarios.context: Topic: short-term effects of caffeine on memory. Three tabs: (A) a 2022 peer-reviewed paper from Journal of Cognitive Psychology, (B) a 2019 personal blog post by a self-described biohacker, (C) a 2024 article on a health magazine site with a sponsored-content tag.

steps.title: Which source do you keep?
steps.prompt: Which of the three sources do you keep for your works-cited?
steps.coachHint: Author, evidence, venue, date — the four-question scan.

options.label: Source A — peer-reviewed, named author, recent
options.feedback: Right — A clears all four scan questions.
options.insight: You applied the credibility scan.

options.label: Source B — first-person, feels authentic
options.feedback: Lived experience can be useful, but it's not citable as evidence for your claim.
options.insight: You weighted voice over evidence.

options.label: Source C — the headline matches your thesis
options.feedback: Sponsored content is advertising, even when it looks editorial.
options.insight: You picked the source that agreed with you, not the one that proved your claim.

steps.title: Bringing in a counter
steps.prompt: Your paper needs a counter-view. Which source helps?
steps.coachHint: A counter isn't a source you disagree with — it's an evidence-grounded opposing view.

options.label: A meta-analysis showing mixed results across studies
options.feedback: Exactly — that's a defensible counter that strengthens your paper.
options.insight: You picked counter-evidence, not counter-opinion.

options.label: A Reddit thread with strong opinions
options.feedback: Opinion ≠ counter-evidence.
options.insight: You substituted opinion for evidence.

steps.title: Writing the warrant
steps.prompt: How do you state the warrant tying your evidence to your claim?
steps.coachHint: Make the connection explicit. Don't trust the reader to draw the line.
steps.voicePrompt: Because the peer-reviewed studies show a measurable short-term effect, and the meta-analysis confirms the direction even with variance, the evidence supports my claim that caffeine produces a small but real short-term memory boost.
steps.modelAnswer: Because peer-reviewed studies show a measurable short-term effect and a meta-analysis confirms the direction with variance, the evidence supports a small but real short-term memory boost.

scenarios.title: Conflicting sources in a term paper
scenarios.outcomeType: Manage two credible sources that disagree

welcome.title: Scenario overview
welcome.body: Two credible peer-reviewed studies on your topic disagree. Your draft is due Friday. What do you do with the conflict?
welcome.reassurance: Conflict is a feature, not a bug. Practice the move that handles it.
welcome.expectedOutcome: Synthesize without flattening or cherry-picking.

scenarios.context: Study X (2021): caffeine improves recall by 8% in healthy adults. Study Y (2023): caffeine has no measurable effect on recall, only on alertness. Both peer-reviewed, different methodologies (cued vs. free recall).

steps.title: Why might they disagree?
steps.prompt: Which is the most defensible read of why X and Y disagree?
steps.coachHint: Methodology, sample, definition — that's usually where conflict comes from.

options.label: Different recall tasks (cued vs. free) measure different things
options.feedback: Exactly — the construct being measured isn't identical.
options.insight: You identified the methodological difference.

options.label: One of them is wrong; pick the more recent one
options.feedback: Recency isn't a methodology argument.
options.insight: You used a heuristic instead of a methodology read.

options.label: Average the two effects together
options.feedback: You'd be averaging across different measures — that doesn't combine.
options.insight: You flattened the difference instead of explaining it.

steps.title: Frame the conflict in your paper
steps.prompt: How do you present the conflict in your draft?
steps.voicePrompt: Studies X and Y reach different conclusions, but the difference reflects the recall measure used. X's cued-recall design captures retrieval support, while Y's free-recall design isolates encoding. Both are credible; they're answering different questions.
steps.coachHint: Name both. Cite both. Write the warrant for which question your paper answers.
steps.modelAnswer: Studies X and Y reach different conclusions, but the difference reflects the recall measure used — X's cued-recall design captures retrieval support, while Y's free-recall design isolates encoding. Both are credible.

scenarios.title: Citing across competing evidence
scenarios.outcomeType: Build a defensible citation strategy

welcome.title: Scenario overview
welcome.body: Four sources, three different conclusions. Your job: cite the disagreement, not paper over it.
welcome.reassurance: Adapted from your prior practice on source evaluation and conflict.
welcome.expectedOutcome: Write a citation paragraph that holds the disagreement visibly.

scenarios.context: Your literature review section has four sources. Two support, one is mixed, one opposes. Word count is tight.

steps.title: Order the citations
steps.prompt: How do you order them in your review?
steps.coachHint: Order communicates weight.

options.label: Strongest evidence first, then counter, then synthesis
options.feedback: Clean structure — reader follows the argument.
options.insight: You used order to communicate weight.

options.label: Only cite the two that support your thesis
options.feedback: Selective citation breaks integrity.
options.insight: You hid the conflict.

options.label: Cite in publication date order, no synthesis
options.feedback: Defensible but lazy — no argument, just a list.
options.insight: You listed instead of argued.

steps.title: Handling the opposing study
steps.prompt: How do you treat the opposing study?
steps.coachHint: Cite it. Name it. Engage it.

options.label: Cite it, name the disagreement, explain your warrant for weighting
options.feedback: That's the move — disagreement is a strength, not a liability.
options.insight: You named the conflict and made your reasoning visible.

options.label: Skip it — it's outside your thesis
options.feedback: Omitting evidence you've read breaks integrity.
options.insight: You omitted what disagreed with you.

scenarios.title: New citation & AI-use policy drill
scenarios.outcomeType: Apply the updated rules to a real draft

welcome.title: Scenario overview
welcome.body: Your university just changed two things: citation format and the rules for AI tool use. Apply them to a real draft.
welcome.reassurance: Five minutes. We'll walk the new rules with you.
welcome.expectedOutcome: Apply the new rules to a paragraph cleanly.

scenarios.context: Draft paragraph contains: a paraphrased peer-reviewed source, a direct quote, and a sentence you generated with an AI tool then revised heavily.

steps.title: Disclose the AI sentence?
steps.prompt: Under the new policy, what do you do with the AI-assisted sentence?
steps.coachHint: Most new policies require disclosure regardless of revision depth.

options.label: Add an AI-use disclosure footnote describing the tool and your edits
options.feedback: Right — disclose, describe, and document.
options.insight: You followed the disclosure rule.

options.label: Leave it as is — you revised it heavily
options.feedback: Revision depth isn't the test; disclosure is.
options.insight: You substituted effort for disclosure.

steps.title: Apply the new format
steps.prompt: The new format requires DOI in the in-text citation for peer-reviewed work. What do you do?

options.label: Add the DOI to the in-text citation; update the works-cited entry
options.feedback: Right — apply both places.
options.insight: You applied the format change consistently.

options.label: Only update the works-cited; in-text stays the old way
options.feedback: Half the change — partial credit only.
options.insight: You half-applied the new format.

scenarios.title: Shift walkthrough · spot the hazards
scenarios.outcomeType: Recognize and decide on three floor hazards

welcome.title: Scenario overview
welcome.body: Walk the floor at shift start. Three hazards are sitting in plain sight. Decide on each: flag, fix, or escalate.
welcome.reassurance: Rehearsal, not test. You can ask the coach for a hint at any step.
welcome.expectedOutcome: Three clean decisions, each defensible.

scenarios.context: Production floor, 6:50 AM. You're 10 minutes before shift start. You see: (1) a coolant puddle near a CNC, (2) an unlabeled solvent container near a hot work area, (3) a coworker without safety glasses inspecting a conveyor.

steps.title: What do you do?
steps.prompt: Coolant puddle near a running CNC. Flag, fix, or escalate?
steps.coachHint: Slip + machine = energy + injury risk.

options.label: Place a wet-floor sign, then escalate to shift lead
options.feedback: Right — immediate mitigation + escalation.
options.insight: You mitigated and reported in the right order.

options.label: Mop it up yourself before shift start
options.feedback: Defensible only if the source is identified — otherwise you've masked a leak.
options.insight: You may have hidden the source of the leak.

options.label: Walk past — production is starting soon
options.feedback: That's how someone gets hurt in the first 10 minutes of shift.
options.insight: You normalized a hazard you saw.

steps.title: Unlabeled container near hot work
steps.prompt: Unlabeled solvent near a hot work area. What do you do?
steps.coachHint: Two rule-breaks at once — HazCom + ignition control.

options.label: Move the container clear of the hot work zone, then escalate immediately
options.feedback: Right — distance first, then reporting.
options.insight: You acted on the bigger risk first.

options.label: Try to identify the contents by smell
options.feedback: Never identify chemicals by smell.
options.insight: You exposed yourself to identify a hazard.

options.label: Leave it — it's not your area
options.feedback: Safety isn't an area; it's a culture.
options.insight: You scoped the hazard out of your concern.

steps.title: Coworker without safety glasses
steps.prompt: How do you handle the PPE gap?
steps.coachHint: Direct, brief, not embarrassing.

options.label: Walk over, hand them the spare pair, low-key
options.feedback: Best move — fix the gap without making it public.
options.insight: You fixed the hazard without escalating the social cost.

options.label: Report them to the shift lead without saying anything
options.feedback: Reporting is fine, but a direct word would have closed the gap faster.
options.insight: You skipped the easier intervention.

options.label: Ignore — it's their decision
options.feedback: PPE isn't optional; speaking up is your job.
options.insight: You let a peer take a risk you could have prevented.

scenarios.title: Near-miss · equipment malfunction
scenarios.outcomeType: Near-miss response and documentation

steps.title: First move
steps.prompt: What do you do first?

options.feedback: Right — preserve the data while it's accurate.
options.insight: You captured the data window.

options.label: Reset the guard and resume — production is behind
options.feedback: You'd be ignoring the cause and losing the data.
options.insight: You prioritized throughput over learning.

options.label: Tell the shift lead at the end of shift

options.insight: You delayed escalation past the useful window.

steps.title: Write the near-miss
steps.prompt: Write the near-miss report — under 60 seconds.
steps.voicePrompt: Conveyor two, fourteen-thirty, guard opened mid-run during normal operation, operator hit e-stop within one second, no injury, three witnesses, line tagged out pending inspection.
steps.coachHint: What happened, when, who saw, what you did, what's outstanding.

scenarios.title: Pattern-read on the floor
scenarios.outcomeType: Spot the setup for the next incident

welcome.title: Scenario overview
welcome.body: Three signals on the floor. None alone is an incident. Together they're a setup. Name the risk before it happens.
welcome.reassurance: Adapted from your prior practice on hazard recognition.
welcome.expectedOutcome: Predict the contributing pattern, escalate ahead of it.

steps.title: What's the risk read?
steps.prompt: Which read best names the contributing pattern?
steps.coachHint: It's not the cable alone — it's the cable + new operator + overtime.

options.label: New operator + worn cable + overtime = elevated risk on Line 3 next 48h
options.feedback: Right — three contributing factors compound.
options.insight: You named the pattern, not the part.

options.label: The cable needs replacing — fix that, problem solved
options.feedback: True but incomplete. You'd still have a new operator working under deadline pressure.
options.insight: You closed one factor and missed the system.

options.label: No risk — overtime is normal
options.feedback: Normal isn't safe.
options.insight: You normalized the conditions.

steps.title: What do you escalate?
steps.prompt: Compose the escalation to the EHS lead.
steps.voicePrompt: Line three has a contributing pattern over the next forty-eight hours, new operator working with a worn auxiliary feeder cable under overtime conditions, recommending cable replacement and a brief refresher with the new operator before they continue shift.
steps.modelAnswer: Line 3, next 48h: new operator + worn aux feeder cable + overtime push. Recommend cable replacement and a brief refresher with the new operator before continuing.

scenarios.title: Hazard escalation drill — post-incident
scenarios.outcomeType: Apply the updated escalation pathway

welcome.title: Scenario overview
welcome.body: After last week's Line 3 near-miss, EHS updated the escalation pathway. Run it.
welcome.reassurance: Short drill. Apply the new pathway cleanly.
welcome.expectedOutcome: Use the new escalation thresholds and timing.

scenarios.context: You're walking the floor 30 minutes after a coworker reports a sticky e-stop on Line 5. They've already tagged it. Production lead wants to keep running.

steps.title: Do you hold the line?
steps.prompt: Under the new pathway, what do you do?
steps.coachHint: Old pathway allowed continued operation with monitoring. New pathway does not.

options.label: Hold the line until E-stop is verified or replaced
options.feedback: Right — new pathway zeros out the 'monitor and run' option.
options.insight: You applied the new threshold.

options.label: Keep running with a designated watcher
options.feedback: That's the old pathway. New pathway closed this loophole.
options.insight: You ran the old pathway.

scenarios.title: An odd message in class chat
scenarios.outcomeType: Decide what to do with a message that lands wrong

welcome.title: Scenario overview
welcome.body: Someone in your class chat sent a message that feels mean. It's about another student. Decide what to do.
welcome.reassurance: There's no wrong move that lasts forever. We're practicing the first move.
welcome.expectedOutcome: Pause, document, talk to an adult — without making it worse.

scenarios.context: Class chat, after school. A classmate posts something embarrassing about another student. Several thumbs-ups. Some kids laughing.

steps.title: Your first action
steps.prompt: What do you do first?
steps.coachHint: Pause before you type.

options.label: Screenshot the message and step away from the chat
options.feedback: Right — you preserved the evidence and bought yourself a second.
options.insight: You paused and preserved.

options.label: Reply telling them to stop
options.feedback: Brave, but it can escalate online. The adult can do this better.
options.insight: You took on a job that adults handle better.

options.label: Add a laughing emoji to fit in
options.feedback: Now you're part of it.
options.insight: You joined the harm.

steps.title: Who do you tell?
steps.prompt: Who do you tell first?

options.label: A trusted adult — parent, teacher, or counselor
options.feedback: Right — adults are equipped to handle this.
options.insight: You routed it to someone with the right tools.

options.label: Your best friend, then maybe an adult later

options.insight: You stopped short of the action that matters.

options.label: Nobody — it's not your business
options.feedback: If you saw it, it's your business.
options.insight: You stayed silent on something you saw.

scenarios.title: Group project · conflict in the docs
scenarios.outcomeType: Resolve a conflict in a shared doc

welcome.title: Scenario overview
welcome.body: Your group project is due Friday. One person isn't doing the work, another is rewriting everyone else's section. Comments are getting tense.
welcome.reassurance: Different setup, same skills — communicate without making it worse.
welcome.expectedOutcome: Move the conflict toward resolution, not escalation.

scenarios.context: Shared doc. You've contributed your section. One groupmate hasn't shown up online in 3 days. Another just deleted someone's paragraph and replaced it without comment.

steps.title: Respond to the deletion
steps.prompt: How do you respond?

options.label: Comment: "Can you share why you replaced this? Want to align before we keep editing."
options.feedback: Calm, curious, scoped. That's the move.
options.insight: You opened with a question, not a charge.

options.label: Undo the change and add a sharp comment
options.feedback: Now you're in an editing war.
options.insight: You escalated the format instead of the conversation.

options.label: Tag the teacher with the screenshot
options.feedback: Defensible later, but skip the in-group attempt and you'll get a reputation for snitching.
options.insight: You skipped the peer step.

steps.title: The teammate who's gone
steps.prompt: What do you do about the groupmate who hasn't shown up?

options.label: DM them once asking if they're okay and offering to catch them up
options.feedback: Right — human first, work second.
options.insight: You checked on the person before the deliverable.

options.label: Tell the teacher they aren't doing the work
options.feedback: Defensible if it's late, but you skipped checking in.
options.insight: You went to the deliverable before the human.

options.label: Ignore — they'll come back when they're ready
options.feedback: Project's Friday. Quiet isn't a strategy.
options.insight: You waited past the useful window.

scenarios.title: Using an AI tool — should you?
scenarios.outcomeType: Decide on AI use under your class's rules

welcome.title: Scenario overview
welcome.body: You're stuck on a science write-up. You have an AI tool that can write the intro paragraph for you. Decide what to do.
welcome.reassurance: Adapted from your prior practice. You've already shown the foundation.
welcome.expectedOutcome: Decide using the three-question check.

steps.title: Decide
steps.prompt: What do you do?
steps.coachHint: Allowed for this? Credits original? Teacher would recognize you?

options.feedback: Right — uses the tool inside the rule.
options.insight: You used the tool inside the rule.

options.label: Let AI write the intro, then change a few words
options.feedback: That's the rule-break.
options.insight: You crossed the line by relabeling AI work as your own.

options.label: Don't use AI at all, even though it's allowed for brainstorming
options.feedback: Safe but you're leaving a legal tool on the table.
options.insight: You opted out of a tool the rules allowed.

scenarios.title: New class platform · same rules?
scenarios.outcomeType: Apply the new platform's rules

welcome.title: Scenario overview
welcome.body: Your district just switched class platforms. The norms for messaging changed. Try the new flow.
welcome.reassurance: Short drill. The skill carries over.
welcome.expectedOutcome: Use the new posting norms cleanly.

steps.title: Where does this go?
steps.prompt: You want to ask a classmate why they didn't show up to a group meeting. Public post or DM?

options.label: DM — it's between you two
options.feedback: Right — private question, private channel.

scenarios.title: A student's behavior is changing
scenarios.outcomeType: Recognize a cluster and decide on next step

welcome.title: Scenario overview
welcome.body: A normally bright student is missing more days, withdrawing, and made a passing comment about home. Each alone is a maybe. Together they're a cluster.
welcome.reassurance: We're rehearsing the move, not deciding the case.
welcome.expectedOutcome: Recognize the cluster and route it through your reporting path.

scenarios.context: Mid-semester. 7th grader Jamie: three absences in two weeks, hood-up in class, said "I don't want to go home today" on Wednesday in passing. Otherwise quiet.

steps.title: What do you call this?
steps.prompt: How do you frame what you're seeing?
steps.coachHint: Cluster, not certainty.

options.label: A cluster of changes that warrants a conversation and a report
options.feedback: Right — pattern + comment = lowered threshold.
options.insight: You named the pattern correctly.

options.label: Probably just a rough month — keep watching
options.feedback: Watching alone is what closes the window.
options.insight: You softened the signal.

options.label: A reportable case — pull them from class immediately

options.insight: You overcorrected on intensity.

steps.title: First conversation
steps.prompt: You decide to check in. What's your opener?

options.feedback: Right — the threshold is reasonable suspicion, which you have.
options.insight: You filed inside the threshold.

options.label: No — wait for more evidence
options.feedback: Waiting is the failure mode that costs the most.
options.insight: You delayed past the useful window.

scenarios.title: Confidentiality, documentation, escalation
scenarios.outcomeType: Manage a complex disclosure

welcome.title: Scenario overview
welcome.body: A student tells you something in confidence that you're required to escalate. Balance trust, documentation, and the right path.
welcome.reassurance: Different student, different shape — same skill family.
welcome.expectedOutcome: Hold the student's trust while doing the required next step.

scenarios.context: After class, an 8th grader confides about something happening at home that meets reportable threshold. They ask you not to tell anyone.

steps.title: What do you say?
steps.prompt: How do you respond?

options.label: "I hear you. I have to tell someone who can help — that's not optional for me. We'll do it together if you want."

options.insight: You held trust and the mandate simultaneously.

options.label: Promise to keep it secret so they keep talking

Who you escalated to and when

scenarios.title: Documenting under pressure
scenarios.outcomeType: Tight documentation in a complex case

welcome.title: Scenario overview
welcome.body: A parent meeting got heated. Document it cleanly enough that any reviewer can read it cold.
welcome.reassurance: Adapted from your prior practice on disclosure and documentation.

scenarios.title: Updated state reporting requirements

welcome.reassurance: Short drill. Same core skill.

scenarios.title: IV Math · Drug calculations
